This is simultaneously assertive, affirmative, and positive; three options describe it, so the item has no unique answer.
It is both a simple sentence by structure and an assertive sentence by function. The choices mix these classification systems, so more than one is correct.
Both C and D are grammatical. The choices do not establish a unique error-free sentence.
The reason does not determine a unique frequency: rarely and occasionally (among other readings) can both fit. The item is held.
“In case of emergencies” is a prepositional phrase, not a clause, because it has no subject and finite verb. None of the listed clause types applies.
Both “have any problem searching” and “have any problem in searching” are grammatical. The choices do not give a unique completion.
Elaborate means detailed as an adjective, or explain in detail as a verb. The noun explanation is related but is not a grammatical synonym; no accurate synonym is supplied.
Implicit means implied rather than explicitly stated, or inherent in another sense. Explicit is absent; specific is related to precision but is not a reliable opposite without context.

heldItems.reason: As of the August 2024 sitting, the Lok Sabha had 543 elected seats; none of the choices gives that number. The historical figure 545 includes two nominated Anglo-Indian members, a provision that had ceased to operate. Do not score this outdated item.
Both Kelvin and Rankine are absolute temperature scales whose zero corresponds to absolute zero. Since both appear among the choices, the printed item has more than one correct answer and is held.

None of the choices expresses past ability. Option A is present ability ('can'), B is expectation ('should have'), C is past habit ('would always'), D is future ('will need'). The expected modal for past ability would be 'could.' The item has no correct option and remains unscored.

No option expresses a past obligation. Option A is present advice ('should take'), B is present obligation ('must finish'), C is past ability ('could run'), D is past habit ('would always help'). The expected form for past obligation would be 'had to.' The item has no correct option and remains unscored.

Options A and B are both 'to' and both correctly complete the sentence ('She is allergic to cats'). Because the item requires one answer index but prints duplicate correct choices, it is defective and remains unscored.
Both B (“bigger than”) and D (“more fluently than”) correctly use comparative forms. The question asks for a single correct sentence but provides two, so it is held.
Both B (a correctly punctuated list) and D (a comma joining two independent clauses with “but”) are grammatically punctuated. The single-answer item is ambiguous and is held.

Each option can be reordered into a grammatical sentence (for example, “She found an interesting book yesterday” and “The children played happily in the park”). The item has multiple correct choices and is held.
All four word groups can be reordered into grammatical sentences. The item has multiple correct choices and is held.

The official final key has no answer for this item. Option D is the likely direct-speech conversion if the two uses of "they" refer to the same people, but the item is held out because that reference is unstated.
